D011-D012_h005.question_both:
I’ve been feeling really on edge lately—like my body can’t relax, even when I’m not doing anything. It’s hard to sit still sometimes; I feel this constant buzz, like I’m wound too tight. My shoulders and the back of my neck are always knotted up, and I’ve had these dull headaches that won’t go away. I massage them, stretch, take breaks, but nothing helps for long.

At school, little things keep popping into my head—like what if I miscounted the kids during a fire drill, or forgot to lock the classroom door after dismissal. These thoughts just crash in while I’m reading to the kids or grading papers. I start imagining the worst—like someone could get hurt because of me, even though I know that sounds extreme. I try to push it away, but it lingers.

There are moments when just *thinking* about certain situations—like being responsible for something going wrong—makes my chest get tight. I can’t explain why it bothers me so much. My husband says I’m overthinking, but it’s not that simple. I don’t know if it’s everything all at once or just one thing I can’t name.
D011-D012_h005.question_a:
I’ve been feeling completely on edge for months—like my mind won’t shut off. At school, if I misplace a worksheet or a lesson doesn’t go perfectly, I immediately think, *What if the parents complain? What if I get written up? What if I lose my job and can’t support my family?* These thoughts just crash into my mind, even when I’m trying to grade papers or read to my students. I can’t sit still—my legs jiggle, I pace between classes, and my shoulders and neck are always tight, like I’m carrying bricks. Some of my coworkers have noticed I look “wound up.”  

I do get really anxious around needles—like during blood draws—but that’s not what’s disrupting my life. The truth is, I worry about everything: my husband’s health, my students’ progress, deadlines, money, even whether I locked the front door three times after leaving. It’s not just one thing; it’s like a constant hum of dread across every part of my day. I can’t point to just one fear—it’s all of it, all the time.
D011-D012_h005.question_b:
I’ve been feeling really on edge lately, but it’s not like I’m worried about everything—it’s just this one thing. Ever since I had to chaperone a field trip to the science museum last spring, where we took the elevator to the top floor, I can’t stop thinking about it. The moment the doors closed, my heart started pounding, my palms got sweaty, and I was absolutely convinced the cable would snap and we’d plummet. I know that sounds irrational, but in the moment, it feels so real. Now, even the thought of getting on an elevator makes my shoulders and neck tighten up something awful—sometimes I get headaches from the tension.

I don’t worry like this about my classroom, my students, or my family. Actually, teaching keeps me pretty grounded. But anything involving elevators—office buildings, hospitals, even big department stores—I avoid completely. I’ll take the stairs no matter how many flights. My husband doesn’t understand why I can’t just “get over it,” but it’s not just nervousness—it’s this sudden, overwhelming fear that hits only in those moments. Otherwise, I feel completely fine.

- **Key Difference:** Scope and characteristics of anxiety
- **Rule for Target (Specific Phobia):** ['Intense fear and anxiety limited only to specific objects or situations appear, and anxiety does not appear in other areas.']
- **Rule for Differential (Generalized Anxiety Disorder):** ['Extensive anxiety and worry appear across various areas of daily life (work, school, health, family, etc.), not just specific objects.']
